teaser: A soldier, a nursing mother, a bolt of lightning. Five centuries on, nobody knows the story.
review_notes:
Size 83 x 73 cm (Accademia gives about 82 x 73).
Michiel's 1530 note in Gabriele Vendramin's house, wording paraphrased: little landscape on canvas with the storm, the gypsy and the soldier.
X-ray (Morassi, 1939) showing a seated nude woman bathing at lower left; the marker position for her is approximate.
The white bird on the roof is usually called a stork or heron; identification is not certain.
Acquired by the Italian state for the Accademia in 1932 from the Giovanelli family.
Claim that only a handful of paintings are securely Giorgione's (number debated).
Catalog year 1508 is a conventional approximate date; the painting is undated.

lesson.text: This canvas is 83 centimeters tall and 73 wide, about 33 by 29 inches. You could carry it under one arm. Around 1508 that was an odd size for an ambitious Venetian picture: far too small for a church, and with no saint in it anyway. It was made to hang in a private room and be looked at slowly.

Its owner was Gabriele Vendramin, a rich Venetian with a house full of antiquities. In 1530 a visitor named Marcantonio Michiel listed what he saw there. For this picture he wrote, more or less: a little landscape on canvas, with a storm, a gypsy woman and a soldier. That is the oldest description we have. Notice that it gives no story.
Michiel was writing only about twenty years after the paint dried, in the home of the man who probably ordered the picture. Even then, he named the weather before he named the people.

He had his priorities right. The two figures are pushed to the edges, and the middle of the picture is given to a river, a bridge, a town and a sky turning the color of a bruise. Before you meet the people, test how carefully Giorgione built that town.
A white bird is standing on one of the rooftops. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The rooftop bird
spots.text: A long-necked white bird, usually read as a stork or heron, perches on the ridge of the roof right under the storm. A speck of calm, one hand's width from the lightning.

lesson.text: You probably passed the lightning on your way there. It is one of the earliest bolts in Western painting that looks like real weather and not like a symbol. The flash explains the strange light: the walls of the town glow pale while the sky behind them is dark, as happens in the second before thunder.
Now the people. Michiel called them a soldier and a gypsy, but he was guessing like everyone since. Check his words against what Giorgione actually painted.

lesson.title: The cast
lesson.text: Three things stand in the foreground: a man, a woman, and a ruin between them.

spots.title: The “soldier”
spots.text: He carries a long staff, not a weapon, and wears no armor: a short red jacket and a white shirt. He stands relaxed, weight on one leg, head turned toward the other bank.

spots.title: The mother
spots.text: Naked except for a white cloth over her shoulders, she nurses a baby. She does not look at the child or at the man. Her eyes are on you.

spots.title: Broken columns
spots.text: Two column stumps stand on a brick base. Nothing rests on them. They belong to no building in the picture, like a prop left on a stage.

lesson.text: So: a man who watches, a woman who watches you, and a stream running between them. They never meet. Scholars have proposed Adam and Eve after Eden, the infant Paris found by shepherds, the Holy Family resting on the way to Egypt, and virtues such as Fortitude and Charity. There are dozens of readings, and none has won.
The Tempest may be the first famous painting in Europe whose subject is a mood. The weather is not a backdrop for the story. The weather is the story.

In 1939 the picture was X-rayed, and the puzzle got deeper. Under the paint at the lower left, close to where the man stands, there is a second woman: seated, naked, dipping her legs in the water. Giorgione painted her, changed his mind, and covered her.

That hidden bather tells you how he worked. A painter illustrating a fixed story does not swap a woman for a man halfway through. Giorgione seems to have composed directly on the canvas, in oil paint, shifting things until the picture felt right. Florentine artists, who planned everything in drawings first, found this Venetian habit shocking.

Giorgione came from Castelfranco, a small walled town on the mainland near Venice. He died in 1510, during an outbreak of plague, when he was only in his early thirties. Very few paintings are accepted as his by everyone, and almost every one of them is argued over.

His method needed a soft touch. Edges melt: the trees on the right dissolve into the sky, and the grass has no outline at all. Color does the work that line did for earlier painters. Greens and blue-greens fill most of the surface, so the few warm notes, the red jacket and the pale skin, ring out.

spots.title: The lightning
spots.text: A thin, crooked stroke of yellow-gold in a tear in the clouds. It lights the cloud edges around it, and nothing in the picture reacts.

spots.title: The bridge
spots.text: A plain wooden footbridge on posts, the only link between the two banks. Nobody is on it.

spots.title: Her gaze
spots.text: Head tilted, lips closed, she looks straight out of the picture. It is the only pair of eyes that meets yours.

spots.title: The vanished bather
spots.text: X-rays found a seated nude woman painted in this lower left zone, bathing her legs, before Giorgione covered her over. Nothing of her shows on the surface today.

spots.title: His face
spots.text: Half in shadow under dark curls, turned to the right. Is that a smile? He seems in no hurry to get out of the rain that is coming.

spots.title: A ruined wall
spots.text: Behind the man, a pale wall with blind arches crumbles into the bushes. Ruins on his side, a lived-in town on the far side.

lesson.text: The painting stayed in private Venetian palaces for more than four hundred years. The Italian state bought it only in 1932 and gave it to the Accademia, where it has hung ever since.

People who stand in front of it today tend to do what Michiel did in 1530. They list what is there, a storm, a woman, a man, and then they stop, because the picture gives nothing more. Was there ever a key, shared between the painter and Gabriele Vendramin and then lost? Or did the two of them want a picture with no answer?

quiz.question: What did Marcantonio Michiel see in the picture in 1530?
options: The Holy Family in a storm
A landscape with a storm, a gypsy and a soldier
quiz.explanation: His note names the landscape and the weather, then a gypsy and a soldier, and tells no story.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal under the man's side of the painting?
quiz.explanation: Giorgione first painted a bather at the lower left, then covered her.

quiz.question: Where does the nursing woman look?
options: At the man across the stream
quiz.explanation: Her eyes meet yours, not the child's or the man's.

quiz.question: What is the man holding?
quiz.explanation: He has a staff and no armor, which makes “soldier” a doubtful label.

quiz.question: How did Giorgione's working method differ from Florentine practice?
options: He composed and changed things directly on the canvas
He drew every figure on paper first
quiz.explanation: The covered bather shows him revising as he painted.

facts.text: The Tempest was painted as an altarpiece for a Venetian church.
facts.explanation: It is a small canvas made for the private house of Gabriele Vendramin.

facts.text: The painting entered a public museum only in 1932.
facts.explanation: It stayed in Venetian palaces until the Italian state bought it for the Accademia.

facts.text: Scholars have agreed since the 1500s that the picture shows Adam and Eve.
facts.explanation: That is only one of dozens of readings, and none is accepted by everyone.
